analysis.one_liner: Makes airlines refund fees for lost bags and undelivered services, disclose fees upfront, and stop shrinking seats.
analysis.headline: Introduced on May 19, 2016 with two Democratic cosponsors, the bill never got so much as a subcommittee vote and died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have forced airlines to automatically refund baggage fees when bags arrive late and refund any fee for a service a passenger never received. It would have required airlines and ticket agents to show baggage, change, cancellation, and seat-selection fees in a standard format before purchase, and it would have frozen seat size, legroom, and aisle width while the FAA wrote minimum space standards. It also added help for passengers with disabilities, families of crash victims, and parents traveling with young children.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers. Anyone whose bag shows up late would get their baggage fee back automatically; anyone whose flight is canceled would get fees refunded for services they never received. Travelers would see all major airline fees displayed in plain language before buying, would be told that paying for a seat assignment is optional, and parents would be told whether their child under 13 can sit next to them for free. Passengers with disabilities would get a dedicated advisory committee, studies of cabin wheelchair restraints and airport access, and a review of airline staff training. Families of people killed in crashes of any size — not just major disasters — would qualify for airline family assistance, and victims on the ground would be covered too.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Air travelers, especially families and disabled passengers

how_it_helps.text: Airlines would have to automatically refund baggage fees if a checked bag is not delivered within 6 hours of a domestic flight's arrival or 12 hours after an international flight, and refund any ancillary fee for a service the passenger does not receive, including on flights the passenger cancels.

Airlines and ticket agents would have to disclose baggage, cancellation, change, ticketing, and seat-selection fees in a standardized format, prominently displayed before purchase online and stated by phone before purchase.

The FAA would be barred from letting airlines shrink seat size, padding, legroom, or aisle width, would have to write minimum space standards for passenger safety, health, and comfort, and airlines would have to post their seat dimensions on their websites.

Travelers would be told at the point of sale that paid seat selection is optional, parents would be told whether adjoining seats for children under 13 are free, airlines would have to point customers to the Transportation Department's complaint process, and DOT would have to build a searchable complaint database and a free mobile app for passenger rights.
Airline obligations to assist families after a crash would extend from major accidents to any fatal accident, including victims on the ground.

Passengers with disabilities would gain a new DOT advisory committee on air travel barriers, a study of in-cabin wheelchair restraint systems, and government reviews of airport accessibility and airline staff training.

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, which would owe automatic refunds, restructure how they display fees, and stop packing more seats onto planes; ticket agents and online booking sites, which would have to display the standardized fee and seat information. Some of the seat-density cost could show up as somewhat higher fares, since planes carrying fewer seats spread costs across fewer passengers. Taxpayers would fund the studies, reports, and the DOT app.

drawbacks.text: Most of the bill directs studies, reviews, and future rulemakings rather than immediate rules: the refunds and disclosures would come a year or more after enactment, if the Transportation Department acted on schedule at all.

The Department of Transportation could soften the baggage-refund deadlines if it finds them unfeasible — up to 12 hours for domestic bags and 24 hours for international ones — and the bill explicitly preserves airlines' discretion over which flights to cancel in bad weather.

Freezing seat size and writing minimum space standards would force planes to carry fewer passengers, a cost airlines would likely pass along in fares; the bill itself orders a study of how airlines set change and cancellation fees rather than capping them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections have clear dollar value for travelers — automatic fee refunds and upfront fee disclosure are things passengers currently have to fight for one complaint at a time, and the seat-size freeze would stop a real trend toward tighter cabins. But the bill is weaker than its title suggests: much of it is paperwork — reviews, reports, and advisory committees — and its biggest rules would be written later by a Department of Transportation whose own enforcement record the bill concedes needs studying. The seat rules could nudge fares up. On balance a net gain for travelers, but a gradual and partially discretionary one.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee within two days of introduction, neither ever took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Thompson introduced the Airline Consumer Protection Act of 2016 in the House on May 19, 2016.
That same day the bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and on May 20 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Aviation.
No further action was ever recorded — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines came out ahead: by the bill dying in subcommittee, they never faced the automatic refund mandates, standardized fee disclosures, or the freeze on shrinking seat size, and travelers got none of the promised protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, which never faced the new rules

for.name: Rep. Mike Thompson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Airline Consumer Protection Act of 2016 in the House on May 19, 2016.

against.name: Rep. Bill Shuster
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired took the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or vote on it.

against.name: House Aviation Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 20, 2016 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no split was recorded; the only members on record supporting the bill were its Democratic sponsor and two Democratic cosponsors, and the Republican-chaired committee of jurisdiction never acted.

industries.note: The bill would force automatic refunds of baggage and other fees, standardized upfront fee display, and a freeze on shrinking seats and legroom — all costs and lost flexibility for carriers that profit from fees and denser cabins. Its death left airlines free of all of it.

industries.industry: Online travel agencies and ticket agents
industries.note: Booking sites and agents would have had to display each airline's baggage, change, cancellation, and seat fees in a standardized format before purchase, a compliance burden their customers would have benefited from.
